newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish credit growth data won't hit bonds - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish credit growth data won't hit bonds - analysts.

text.p: Thursday's higher-than-expected Irish credit growth figures for August may cause short-term jitters in the bond market but are unlikely to do any real damage to prices, analysts said.
Dealers said that although Irish bonds sank in late trade on Thursday, this was mostly due to profit-taking after a recent rapid climb rather than to any negative impact from the credit growth data.
"The figures won't be ignored and initially the short end and cash rates are going to tighten," said Pat O'Sullivan of AIB Capital Markets.
"But I think the natural momentum of the bond market and cash market will brush the figures aside, maybe as quickly as tomorrow morning," he said.
Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers, said the figures would have little impact.
"The numbers were marginally higher than we expected but I don't think they are high enough to cause the convergence theme any great harm," he said.
The adjusted annual rate of Irish private sector credit growth climbed to 14.3 percent in August from 13.8 percent in July, according to central bank figures.
By 1630 GMT the eight percent bond due 2000 was down 30p at 107.05 to yield 5.90 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 fell 45p to 107.85, yielding 6.76 percent.
"Part of the decline came before the numbers and we've seen prices marked down since the numbers," a dealer said. "We're not surprised by a bit of profit-taking at this stage."
O'Sullivan said buying of Irish bonds on EMU convergence trades was unlikely to be discouraged by the data.
"Optimism over EMU will predominate over any concerns over the growth of these credit numbers," he said.
"Although these numbers are strong we don't see them translating into any serious inflationary threat for the economy," he said.

Garvey said credit growth was likely to begin falling over the rest of the year. "The September numbers should be helped by a positive year-on-year effect. There were very strong September numbers last year and the year-on-year rates may have peaked. That's something the markets will be happy about," he said.

But Alan McQuaid at Bloxham Stockbrokers said credit growth would continue to accelerate. "We believe that credit demand will keep on growing until the (central) bank steps in again," he said in a research note.
